children.text: A good analysis does not win a decision by itself. The same business case needs to be told differently to a board that governs a hospital, to a payer deciding whether to share savings and to a legislature deciding whether to appropriate money. Chapter 7 ends with implications for each audience; this lesson turns them into a working method.

It starts from the money available to Vermont organizations in 2026 and 2027, which shapes what a case can propose, then sets out what each audience needs to see, how to handle the objections each is likely to raise, and how to write the decision request. The sources for the funding facts are the book and recent press coverage, and the lesson says where a number is the book's alone.
The last section is a one-page template. Lesson 15's capstone uses it.
The Money Available, and Its Limits

Three funding streams shape the cases Vermont organizations can make. The first is the Rural Health Transformation Program, which local reporting says allocates $195 million a year for five years to Vermont, with priorities including primary care, mental health and keeping rural hospitals open. Chapter 7 includes remote monitoring grants from the program in its examples, and Chapter 3 notes the program's national funds, $50 billion, expire in 2030 while Medicaid reductions accelerate afterward. The money is real and time-limited, so a case funded by it needs a plan for what happens after 2030.

The second is the savings the payment system itself creates: shared savings under contracts, margin under global budgets and the savings from reference-based pricing that the statute requires to reach premiums. The third is state appropriations, as the Blueprint's Medicare backfill shows: the legislature can fund a gap, once, if the case is compelling. Each stream has a different timing and a different owner, which matters when a case proposes to sustain a program beyond a grant.
A case funded by time-limited money must show how the program is financed when the money ends: through savings captured, a payer contract or a state appropriation.
The Board: Risk and Capital

A hospital board asks three questions: what does it cost, what is the risk and what happens if we do nothing? The case should lead with the last. Under reference-based pricing, the global budget timeline and H.R. 1, doing nothing has a modeled cost, which the Hospital Financial Stress Test of Lesson 9 quantifies. The proposal then appears as a way to reduce that exposure, not as discretionary spending.

Then it should show the three-case return from Lesson 10 with the share-of-savings adjustment, the payback period and the readiness gaps from Lessons 4 and 5. A board is most persuaded by a plan that spends first on the binding constraint. If the readiness assessment shows revenue cycle at 30 percent, funding care managers before fixing coding and attribution invites a failure the board will later attribute to the proposal.

Finally, state the decision and the control: the amount, the milestones that release each tranche, the measures reported to the board quarterly and the trigger for stopping. Boards approve investments they can steer.

A board will also ask how the proposal fits with commitments already made. Show the capital plan with the proposal in it, the effect on days cash on hand and debt service coverage using the stress test's measures, and the effect on covenants if the first year runs below plan. A proposal that quietly pushes the hospital toward a covenant threshold will be rejected, however strong its long-run return, and it is better for the proposer to raise the issue first and show how the tranches release only as the milestones are met.
The Payer: Alignment and Fairness

A payer wants a contract that reduces its costs without taking on risk it cannot manage. Chapter 7 advises hospital executives to use every commercial contract renewal to negotiate three things: shared savings arrangements that let the hospital capture the benefit of the utilization reduction its investments produce, quality measurement aligned with HEDIS and the Green Mountain Care Board's global budget measures instead of payer-specific measures, and administrative simplification, including consolidated reporting, standardized prior authorization and reduced documentation.

The negotiation uses the contract checklist of Lesson 6. A hospital arguing for a fair benchmark should have its own baseline analysis, a position on rebasing and ratchet protection and a stated view on carve-out symmetry. It should also be ready for the payer's counter-argument, which is that a hospital's savings come from the payer's own price reductions under reference-based pricing. Chapter 7 treats that tension openly: reference-based pricing is itself a savings stream for payers, and the statute requires the Board to monitor that price decreases reach premiums.

Chapter 7 also notes a structural difficulty for the legislature to consider: Vermont's commercial market is concentrated in a small number of large insurers, which creates negotiating dynamics that global budgets do not resolve, and the Board has authority over hospital rates but not over insurer behavior in these negotiations.
The Legislature: Public Value and Accountability

A legislative committee asks different questions again: who benefits, what does it cost the state, how will we know it worked and what happens if it does not? The Blueprint's Medicare backfill is a useful model. The legislature appropriated more than $5 million to cover one year's gap, a decision that rested on the program's established role, its funding structure and the warning that loss of funding could significantly reduce community health team staffing.

A strong legislative case therefore names the beneficiaries and the number of people served, states the appropriation and its duration, shows the measures that will be reported and when, and acknowledges the limits of the evidence. The Blueprint's own annual report, which is candid about what its risk-adjusted comparison does and does not show, is an example of the tone that earns trust. Overstated returns invite the kind of audit critique the program received.

Legislatures also care about equity and geography. A case that shows who is reached, by region and by the groups the state is accountable for, is stronger than one that reports only an average. It should also say what the state would give up by acting later: reference-based pricing and the global budget timetable are statutory, so delay shifts risk to hospitals and, if they fail, to patients and communities.
Objections and the One-Page Case

children.text: The one-page case has six parts. The problem and its cost if unaddressed, with a source. The proposal and its cost, including the financing after any grant. The return as a range, with the evidence rung for each input and the share of savings kept. The readiness and risk position, naming the binding constraint and what is done about it. The measures and the stop trigger. And the decision requested, with the date it is needed. Everything else belongs in an appendix.

body.message: A one-page case that gives one return figure and no range, no share-of-savings adjustment and no financing plan after the grant will not survive a skeptical reader.
body.title: A single number is not a case

points: Vermont's time-limited funding, reported at $195 million a year for five years from the Rural Health Transformation Program, requires a plan for financing after the money ends.
To a board, lead with the modeled cost of doing nothing, show a three-case return with the share of savings kept, and spend first on the binding readiness constraint.
To a payer, use contract renewals to negotiate shared savings, aligned quality measures and administrative simplification, with a clear position on benchmarks and carve-outs.
Reference-based pricing is itself a savings stream for payers, and the statute requires the Board to monitor whether price decreases reach premiums.
To a legislature, name the beneficiaries, the appropriation and duration, the measures and reporting dates, and acknowledge the limits of the evidence.
The Blueprint's Medicare backfill of more than $5 million for 2026 shows a legislature can fund a gap once, when the case is compelling.
A one-page case has six parts: problem, proposal and financing, return as a range, readiness and risk, measures and stop trigger, and the decision requested.

body.explanation: Time-limited funds such as the Rural Health Transformation Program expire, and Chapter 3 notes Medicaid reductions accelerate after 2030. A case that does not show how the program is financed afterward invites the question of what happens when the grant ends.

options.text: Because grant funds always last indefinitely
Because the program must be sustained through captured savings, a payer contract or an appropriation after the money ends, or it will fail when funding stops
Because payers refuse to contract with grant-funded programs
Because financing plans are required by the Green Mountain Care Board for all grants

body.question: Why should a business case funded by time-limited grant money show a post-grant financing plan?
